text: In years when air temperature at 2 m was higher, lake surface temperature (day–night average) tended to be higher: a strong association (r = 0.78, p < 0.001, statistically significant). After removing each series' own straight-line trend, r = 0.68 (p < 0.001, significant). This second number shows whether the two move together from year to year, not just in the same long-term direction.

In years when precipitation over the catchment was higher, lake surface temperature (day–night average) tended to be higher: a weak association (r = 0.26, p = 0.197, not statistically significant). After removing each series' own straight-line trend, r = 0.03 (p = 0.875, not significant). This second number shows whether the two move together from year to year, not just in the same long-term direction.

In years when sunlight reaching the surface was higher, lake surface temperature (day–night average) tended to be higher: a weak association (r = 0.08, p = 0.700, not statistically significant). After removing each series' own straight-line trend, r = 0.08 (p = 0.692, not significant). This second number shows whether the two move together from year to year, not just in the same long-term direction.

In years when surface wind speed was higher, lake surface temperature (day–night average) tended to be higher: a weak association (r = 0.05, p = 0.812, not statistically significant). After removing each series' own straight-line trend, r = -0.21 (p = 0.312, not significant). This second number shows whether the two move together from year to year, not just in the same long-term direction.
